docs.x: Judge Laurel Beeler, N.D. Cal.. Bench trials: Stipulated facts and conclusions of law are due 63 days before the final pretrial conference. Sequential briefs follow: plaintiff’s opening (25 pages) at 49 days before, defendant’s opposition (25 pages) 14 days later, plaintiff’s reply (25 pages) 14 days later, and defendant’s reply (15 pages) 7 days later. Proposed findings must cite trial evidence, and conclusions of law need pincites in Ninth Circuit Manual format, with model instructions relied on cited and any blacklined modifications attached.

Evidence the government thinks favorable but not material must be submitted for in camera review.

Fifth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (latest edition) are preferred. docs.t: Judge Anne T. Berton (W.D. Tex.) — Criminal: 10 days before trial
docs.x: Judge Anne T. Berton, W.D. Tex.. Criminal: 10 days before trial: File each party’s proposed voir dire questions and a joint case summary for the panel; a Joint Motion in Limine (after conferring) showing agreed and disputed items; a Joint Exhibit List showing agreed exhibits and objections, numbered under Local Rule CV-16(h); a witness list; any proposed stipulated facts; and a joint estimate of trial length. Tell the courtroom deputy of any interpreter need for the defendant or a witness. Disputed motion in limine items and exhibits are taken up at a pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Anne T. Berton (W.D. Tex.) — Criminal: technology and trial time limits (trap)

Each party gets 10 minutes for its own voir dire questions, and opening statements are limited to 10 minutes per side (more only in special circumstances, such as multiple defendants).

Hearing exhibits, demonstratives, and slides should be emailed to opposing counsel, the courtroom deputy, and the law clerks at least 2 hours before the hearing.

docs.t: Judge Dan MacLemore (W.D. Tex.) — Scheduling order form (trap)
docs.x: Judge Dan MacLemore, W.D. Tex.. Scheduling order form (trap): Use the judge’s Proposed Scheduling Order template. Fact discovery requests must be served so responses are due by the fact discovery deadline. Claimants make a private written settlement offer and opponents respond in writing by set dates; keep them, because the court uses them in assessing fees and costs. Rule 702 challenges must be made by motion within 14 days after the expert report or deposition, whichever is later; motions more than 14 days after the expert discovery deadline are denied as untimely, and noncompliance waives the objection. Younger attorneys may appear in person as principal advocate while senior counsel appears remotely.

Demonstratives need court approval before the jury sees them and generally are not allowed in voir dire; no exhibit is published without permission. Give the courtroom deputy advance notice of video depositions or use of presentation equipment. All exhibits must be pre-marked at the final pretrial conference; exhibits go to the jury through JERS, following the court’s file-naming and size requirements. docs.x: Judge Dan MacLemore, W.D. Tex.. docs.t: Judge Henry J. Bemporad (W.D. Tex.) — Hearings and remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Henry J. Bemporad, W.D. Tex.. Hearings and remote appearances: The judge typically holds hearings on contested discovery, scheduling, and other non-dispositive civil motions (including arbitration motions and FLSA collective-action notice), default judgment motions, and class certification; usually not on remand, dismissal, or summary judgment motions unless a party requests one. Contested criminal motions and pro se motions to withdraw are typically heard. No set hearing time; civil matters are heard only when the judge is not on criminal duty, and morning settings generally start at 9:00 or 9:30. In-person hearings are preferred, but video hearings are regularly held on request; telephonic hearings are disfavored. Parties must be able to access Zoom beforehand. docs.t: Judge Henry J. Bemporad (W.D. Tex.) — Motions and briefing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Henry J. Bemporad, W.D. Tex.. Motions and briefing (trap): Extra pages beyond the Local Rules require a motion for leave explaining the circumstances. Briefing beyond motion, response, and reply needs leave and a clear showing of good cause, and the judge may rule any time after the response is filed. Letter briefs are usually not accepted except supplemental letters on changed circumstances or new case law. Extensions, even ones that do not affect other dates, should be sought by an agreed motion rather than a stipulation. Criminal motions should follow the Local Rule CV-7 page limits. No courtesy copies and no need to attach cases; bring copies of unreported or important cases to hearings, with extras for opposing counsel.

docs.t: Judge Henry J. Bemporad (W.D. Tex.) — Discovery motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Henry J. Bemporad, W.D. Tex.. Discovery motions (trap): Before filing, consult opposing counsel on each disputed request, and state in the motion or response whether any documents have been withheld based on objections. A motion to compel documentary discovery must attach the opposing party’s responses and objections and identify each disputed item by request number. Before a discovery hearing the judge regularly asks the parties to confer and file a joint advisory on what remains disputed. Parties may contact the judge during depositions on matters requiring immediate attention.

docs.t: Judge Henry J. Bemporad (W.D. Tex.) — Civil scheduling and pretrial
docs.x: Judge Henry J. Bemporad, W.D. Tex.. Civil scheduling and pretrial: In referred cases without a scheduling order, the judge requires scheduling recommendations from all parties, holds a telephonic Initial Pretrial Conference, and then issues a scheduling order. Initial disclosures need not be filed, but their status is checked at that conference. To modify the scheduling order, confer and file an Agreed Motion for Modification of Scheduling Order (or note opposition), specifying the new deadlines. Removed cases must comply with Judge Rodriguez’s Standing Order on removed cases. The scheduling order usually sets a deadline to report the preferred ADR method; mediators are normally chosen by agreement, and a magistrate judge may sometimes mediate. In assigned cases, a final pretrial conference is held a week or two before trial.

docs.t: Judge Henry J. Bemporad (W.D. Tex.) — Criminal practice
docs.x: Judge Henry J. Bemporad, W.D. Tex.. Criminal practice: In assigned misdemeanor cases, a standard scheduling order issues after arraignment or a filed waiver. For continuances, confer and file a motion stating whether it is opposed, the reasons, and the time requested. Conferring is not required on dispositive motions but is the better practice on motions for bond hearings, continuances, expedited hearings, bond modification, and travel; on bond-condition motions confer with both opposing counsel and Pretrial Services, and state the result in the motion’s title and body. Exchange trial exhibits reasonably in advance and raise objections by motion in limine when possible. In misdemeanor cases with a PSR, send objections directly to the probation officer, copying opposing counsel. Contact the courtroom deputy in advance if an evidentiary sentencing hearing is needed.

docs.t: Judge Henry J. Bemporad (W.D. Tex.) — Courtroom and recording (trap)
docs.x: Judge Henry J. Bemporad, W.D. Tex.. Courtroom and recording (trap): There is no court reporter: proceedings are audio-recorded by the courtroom deputy. For transcripts contact Diana Garcia in the Clerk’s Office (diana_garcia@txwd.uscourts.gov, 210-472-5007). Because of the recording, address the court and question witnesses only from the lectern. Ask leave to approach the bench or witnesses; let opposing counsel finish without interruption; be respectful to staff and especially to pro se litigants. Arrange use of courtroom equipment through the courtroom deputy, and give at least 24 hours’ notice to bring your own audio/visual equipment.

docs.t: Judge Henry J. Bemporad (W.D. Tex.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Henry J. Bemporad, W.D. Tex.. Trial: Trial days generally run from 9:00 or 9:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Brief jury questionnaires must be submitted at least 7 business days before trial. Counsel may conduct limited voir dire after the court’s, with time set in advance; openings commonly run 10–15 minutes. Exchange demonstratives before use, ideally before voir dire (strongly preferred but not required). Deposition testimony may be used by agreement even if the witness is available; provide excerpts to the court during trial for the record. Proposed jury instructions, verdict forms, and findings and conclusions may be filed on ECF or emailed (to Branham in civil cases, Miranda in criminal) in PDF or Word. Move to continue a trial as soon as possible, stating opposition, reasons, and time requested.

docs.x: Judge Miguel A. Torres, W.D. Tex.. Pretrial filings in jury cases (trap): In civil jury cases the judge will try, file the Local Rule CV-16(e)-(f) pretrial materials no later than 14 days before jury selection, unless otherwise ordered. The order does not apply where the judge has the case only on pretrial referral; follow the presiding judge’s procedures then.

docs.t: Judge Miguel A. Torres (W.D. Tex.) — Joint pretrial filing
docs.x: Judge Miguel A. Torres, W.D. Tex.. Joint pretrial filing: One joint document, signed by the parties or their representatives and filed by the plaintiff, must contain the CV-16(e)(2)-(6) and (e)(10) and CV-16(f)(1)-(2) items: a voir dire statement of claims and defenses of no more than ½ page double-spaced; stipulated facts; exhibits (expected versus may offer); witnesses (expected versus may call); deposition designations by page and line; trial length estimate; and objections to deposition designations and exhibits. The document must show where the parties disagree and state each side’s position. Exhibit objections (CV-16(f)(2)) must be incorporated into the exhibit identification (CV-16(e)(4)). As the reproduced rule states, undisclosed exhibit objections other than under Rules 402 and 403 are waived absent good cause.

docs.t: Judge Miguel A. Torres (W.D. Tex.) — Separate pretrial filings
docs.x: Judge Miguel A. Torres, W.D. Tex.. Separate pretrial filings: Each party files separately its proposed voir dire questions, proposed jury instructions and verdict forms, proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law (nonjury trials), and any motions in limine (CV-16(e)(1) and (7)-(9)).

docs.t: Judge Richard B. Farrer (W.D. Tex.) — Contacting chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard B. Farrer, W.D. Tex.. Contacting chambers (trap): Staff are instructed not to discuss substantive matters, including the timing of rulings; do not email or call about anticipated rulings or status. Any request for relief, including a continuance or other scheduling change, must be made by motion. Direct contact with law clerks is appropriate only when initiated or expressly authorized by the court. When necessary, email TXWDml_Chambers_SA_JudgeFarrer@txwd.uscourts.gov, copying opposing counsel on all correspondence except ex parte mediation statements. Scheduling, true emergencies (including during depositions), and advance notice of a TRO or other expedited motion go to (210) 244-5012. If a contested motion is resolved, file an Advisory, and also call the courtroom deputy if the resolution is time sensitive.

docs.t: Judge Richard B. Farrer (W.D. Tex.) — Expedited relief
docs.x: Judge Richard B. Farrer, W.D. Tex.. Expedited relief: Contact the court as early as possible if a TRO or other expedited motion is coming. For an expedited hearing, file a motion explaining the need and the deadline by which relief is needed, and alert the court; expedited hearings are reserved for emergencies.

docs.t: Judge Richard B. Farrer (W.D. Tex.) — Motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard B. Farrer, W.D. Tex.. Motions (trap): Make a good-faith effort to confer on contested non-dispositive motions, meaning speaking in person or by phone, often with more than one or two attempts, and include a certificate of conference where required. Extra pages require a motion for leave; the court values brevity and clarity. Briefing beyond motion, response, and reply only with leave, and the judge may rule any time after the response is filed. Letter briefs are not typically accepted; relief requires a motion. No courtesy copies or attached cases. Put citations in the body text rather than footnotes (string cites in footnotes are fine), and do not ascribe motives to the other side without evidence. Hearings are often held on contested non-dispositive motions; on dispositive motions only case by case.

docs.t: Judge Richard B. Farrer (W.D. Tex.) — Scheduling and extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard B. Farrer, W.D. Tex.. Scheduling and extensions (trap): The judge requests scheduling recommendations and issues a scheduling order from them (or with dates of the judge’s choosing if none are submitted), typically following the assigned district judge’s guidelines, which may override the parties’ preferences. To modify the schedule, confer and file an Agreed Motion for Modification of Scheduling Order (or note opposition in the certificate of conference) with a proposed order listing the new deadlines. Even agreed motions can be denied, and last-minute or post-deadline extension motions are disfavored. Extensions that do not affect other dates should also be sought by agreed motion. Initial disclosures need not be filed.

docs.t: Judge Richard B. Farrer (W.D. Tex.) — Initial pretrial conference and removed cases (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard B. Farrer, W.D. Tex.. Initial pretrial conference and removed cases (trap): Initial Pretrial Conferences are often held in referred and consent cases; the setting order explains what the parties must confer on and report. Be ready to discuss the substance of the case, since the judge may probe the merits to find issues for early resolution or streamlined discovery. Every removed case is evaluated sua sponte for federal jurisdiction, and questions may be raised at the conference. Common errors: misunderstanding how LLC and other entity citizenship is determined, and conflating residence with citizenship.

docs.t: Judge Richard B. Farrer (W.D. Tex.) — Hearings, remote appearances, and decorum
docs.x: Judge Richard B. Farrer, W.D. Tex.. Hearings, remote appearances, and decorum: No telephone conferences. Videoconference hearings are typically reserved for Initial Pretrial Conferences or where good reason is shown; hybrid hearings are possible if one side needs video, after counsel confer. There is no court reporter; proceedings are audio-recorded, so use the lectern to address the court and witnesses. For transcripts call the Clerk’s Office at 210-472-6550. Arrange to use courtroom or your own equipment with the courtroom deputy two or three days in advance. Stand when addressing the court; ask leave to approach the bench or witnesses. Interrupting or speaking out of turn is strongly disfavored, and rudeness to counsel or staff will not be tolerated.

docs.t: Judge Richard B. Farrer (W.D. Tex.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Richard B. Farrer, W.D. Tex.. Trial: Trial days typically run 9:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Jury questionnaires need a motion for leave at least 7 days before trial. Attorney voir dire is not typical (more likely in consent cases); parties may submit questions. Opening times are set at the final pretrial conference. Exchange demonstratives at least 3 days before the final pretrial conference. Depositions of available witnesses may be used only by agreement of all parties, addressed no later than the final pretrial conference; provide excerpts to the court during trial. Proposed jury instructions, verdict forms, and findings and conclusions are filed electronically or emailed to chambers in Word. Move to continue trial as soon as possible, stating opposition, reasons, and time requested; a pending dispositive motion may instead be carried to trial.

docs.t: Judge Richard B. Farrer (W.D. Tex.) — ADR and sanctions
docs.x: Judge Richard B. Farrer, W.D. Tex.. ADR and sanctions: If the parties will mediate, the mediator is typically chosen by agreement; parties may move to have another magistrate judge mediate. Sanctions requests are for egregious conduct; strategic sanctions motions are strongly disfavored, and accusations and characterizations must be supported by evidence.

docs.t: Judge Richard B. Farrer (W.D. Tex.) — Criminal duty ex parte filings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Richard B. Farrer, W.D. Tex.. Criminal duty ex parte filings (trap): When Judge Farrer is duty magistrate judge (or standing in), ex parte submissions such as warrant applications, complaints, § 2703(d) orders, pen register or trap and trace applications, and delayed-notice requests cannot be quietly withdrawn or revised. Approved submissions are docketed, and any submission rejected by the Clerk’s Office, not approved, or replaced before signing is docketed under the same case number, marked as rejected, withdrawn, superseded, or amended.

docs.t: Judge Susan Hightower (W.D. Tex.) — Scheduling order form and modifications (trap)
docs.x: Judge Susan Hightower, W.D. Tex.. Scheduling order form and modifications (trap): Use the judge’s Agreed Scheduling Order form (Case No. 1:__-CV-__-SH). The parties fill in deadlines for the Local Rule CV-88 ADR report, settlement offers, amended pleadings and joinder, experts, discovery, and dispositive motions; the court fills in the pretrial conference (10 a.m.), trial (9 a.m.), and pretrial-submission dates. The dispositive motion deadline, final pretrial conference, and trial date can be changed only by agreed motion; any other deadline in the order may be modified by agreement of the parties. Claimants make a private written settlement offer and opponents respond in writing by set dates; keep them, because the court may use them in assessing fees and costs.

docs.t: Judge Susan Hightower (W.D. Tex.) — Experts (trap)
docs.x: Judge Susan Hightower, W.D. Tex.. Experts (trap): Expert designations are filed, while Rule 26(a)(2)(B) materials are served but not filed: claimants first, then parties resisting claims. Rebuttal experts must be designated and their materials served 15 days after receiving the opposing expert’s report. Rule 702 reliability objections must be made by motion, stating the basis and identifying the testimony, within 11 days after receiving the expert’s report or within 11 days after the expert’s deposition is completed, whichever is later.

docs.t: Judge Susan Hightower (W.D. Tex.) — Discovery and dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Susan Hightower, W.D. Tex.. Discovery and dispositive motions: Counsel may agree to continue discovery past the deadline, but the court will not intervene except in extraordinary circumstances, and no trial setting will be vacated because of post-deadline discovery. Dispositive motions and responses are limited to 20 pages, replies to 10 pages. Responses are due 14 days after service of the motion and replies 7 days after service of the response; the court need not wait for a reply before ruling.

docs.t: Judge Susan Hightower (W.D. Tex.) — Pretrial submissions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Susan Hightower, W.D. Tex.. Pretrial submissions (trap): By the court-set date, each party serves and files: proposed voir dire questions; a joint statement of claims and defenses for voir dire (no longer than one-half page, double-spaced); stipulated facts; exhibit and witness lists (expected versus possible, excluding impeachment); deposition designations by page and line; motions in limine; and a trial length estimate. Jury instructions must be a joint proposed set, after meeting and conferring, in complete format as they would go to the jury; disputed instructions are submitted separately with supporting legal citations. Counsel must review Local Rule AT-5 (Standards for Conduct before the Judge and Jury) before the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Susan Hightower (W.D. Tex.) — Objections to pretrial submissions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Susan Hightower, W.D. Tex.. Objections to pretrial submissions (trap): After the CV-16(f) exchange, confer to resolve objections to exhibits, deposition designations, and motions in limine. Then, by a second court-set date, file exhibit objections with grounds (undisclosed objections, other than under Rules 402 and 403, are waived absent good cause), objections to Rule 32(a) use of designated depositions, and responses to motions in limine. The court may impose Rule 16(f) sanctions for untimely submissions.

docs.t: Judge Susan Hightower (W.D. Tex.) — Newer attorneys
docs.x: Judge Susan Hightower, W.D. Tex.. Newer attorneys: If a lawyer practicing less than 7 years will argue all or part of a ripe motion, contact the courtroom deputy to request oral argument. The court will grant it if practicable, even where it would otherwise rule on the briefs, strongly consider extra time, let more experienced counsel also speak, and ask the other side to reciprocate.

Consent and criminal duty months: With consent the judge can handle trials, dispositive motions, judgment, and post-judgment matters such as fee applications; appeals go directly to the Ninth Circuit. Parties may consent to any of the district’s magistrate judges, not just the assigned one; chambers can help check trial dates. The magistrate judges rotate criminal duty by month and generally do not schedule civil consent trials during their criminal duty month.

docs.t: Judge Wes Reber Porter (D. Haw.) — Trial schedule and conduct (trap)
docs.x: Judge Wes Reber Porter, D. Haw.. Trial schedule and conduct (trap): Jury trial runs 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. daily with no lunch break, and may run later; jury selection day runs 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with lunch from noon to 1:30 p.m. Tardiness that delays trial can draw sanctions. Bench conferences are generally not permitted; raise disputes before trial, at recess, or after the jury leaves. No speaking objections: stand, be concise, and cite the basis or rule. No substantive motions in front of the jury. The court conducts general voir dire; each side then has a maximum of 15 minutes. Meet and confer on demonstrative aids or get leave before use; special equipment needs advance permission. Parties arrange their own interpreters.

docs.t: Judge Wes Reber Porter (D. Haw.) — Witnesses, depositions, and motions in limine
docs.x: Judge Wes Reber Porter, D. Haw.. Witnesses, depositions, and motions in limine: Disclose the next day’s witnesses by the close of each trial day. Motions in limine are due by the Scheduling Order deadline and are generally heard at the final pretrial conference. For disputed deposition designations, give the court and parties a list by noon the day before publication, with two working copies of the full condensed transcript highlighting the disputes. After rulings and before publication, file a declaration attaching the redacted transcript.

Meet and confer on a common set of jury instructions; submit hard copies of proposed instructions and special verdict forms plus Word versions to the orders email. Informal discovery conferences (trap): Available for narrow, discrete, unbriefed disputes (instructions not to answer, protective orders, scheduled depositions, document production), including problems arising during a deposition. docs.t: Judge Laura Fashing (D.N.M.) — Telephone conferences on minor discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Laura Fashing, D.N.M.. Telephone conferences on minor discovery disputes: The judge will take narrow, discrete, unbriefed discovery disputes by telephone, including problems during a deposition; requests to compel answers to a number of interrogatories are not suited to this. Counsel must first confer by telephone or in person (email or letters are not enough), and all parties must agree before anyone calls (505) 348-2360 or emails fashingchambers@nmd.uscourts.gov for an appointment. Simply request the conference, with no argument and no criticism of opposing counsel.

docs.t: Judge Laura Fashing (D.N.M.) — Protective orders and sealing
docs.x: Judge Laura Fashing, D.N.M.. Protective orders and sealing: If all parties agree, file a stipulated motion with the proposed order attached and email a Word copy to the proposed-text address. If opposed, the opponent’s response must propose language resolving its specific objections. A proposed protective order must recite specific facts showing good cause under Rule 26(c), cover only narrowly defined categories (not “all documents a party designates as confidential”), and exempt public or previously non-confidential material. It may not bind non-parties, declare continuing jurisdiction, direct the Clerk to return or destroy filed documents, or bind court personnel or jurors. No blanket sealing provision; the order must acknowledge that it “does not entitle them to seal all confidential information filed with the Court.” Under the model language, a non-filing designating party has 14 day

docs.t: Judge Laura Fashing (D.N.M.) — Jury instructions and voir dire (trap)
docs.x: Judge Laura Fashing, D.N.M.. Jury instructions and voir dire (trap): Meet and confer and file a mutually acceptable set on the substantive claims, or be ready to give a legal basis for each objection; each side files a numbered, annotated set of disputed instructions, and objections are due 3 working days after instructions are due. File the verdict form at the same time. Do not submit stock instructions. List the requested stock instructions from the judge’s page on a separate page; objections to stock instructions are addressed at the pretrial conference. One instruction per page, numbered at the top, with a cover sheet for each set; email everything in Word to fashingchambers@nmd.uscourts.gov. The court conducts initial voir dire from its posted standard questions (objections are heard at the pretrial conference); each party then typically gets 20 minutes. Don’t argue the case or cite

docs.t: Judge Laura Fashing (D.N.M.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Laura Fashing, D.N.M.. Trial: Trial recesses about 5:00 p.m.; have witnesses to fill a full day (9 a.m. to 5 p.m.) or risk a penalty. No recess for a missing witness unless timely subpoenaed. Openings are concise, time-limited, and argument-free; stand a respectful distance from the jury. Plaintiff’s exhibits on yellow labels by number, defendant’s on blue labels by letter; display exhibits with courtroom technology if possible. Counsel operate the Digital Evidence Presentation System; schedule training with courtroom deputy Natalie Maestas (505-348-2071) at least 2 weeks before trial. Highlight deposition excerpts on the court’s copy (plaintiff yellow, defendant blue), and provide a person to read the witness’s answers from the stand.

docs.t: Judge Laura Fashing (D.N.M.) — Courtroom conduct and dress
docs.x: Judge Laura Fashing, D.N.M.. Courtroom conduct and dress: Be seated and ready 5 minutes before the start; requests to move a time on a trailing calendar go to the courtroom deputy. Stand to speak, object, or address the court; use surnames; question from the podium; no speaking objections, and opposing counsel responds only if asked. Phones off; no gum. Attorneys wear suits or similar attire; others wear long pants with a collared shirt, blouse, or sweater, or a dress or skirt (jeans acceptable). No shorts, t-shirts, ripped or revealing clothing, thongs, or hats.

docs.t: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough (D.N.M.) — Informal discovery conferences
docs.x: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough, D.N.M.. Informal discovery conferences: To request a telephonic conference on a discovery dispute (including problems during a deposition), call chambers or email the proposed-text address, summarize the issue in a few sentences, and state whether all parties agree to informal resolution. The judge gives an opinion or inclination at the conference, and the parties may follow up with formal motions. Matters should be narrow; the judge may say an issue is unsuited to informal resolution, in which case a party may file a motion.

docs.t: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough (D.N.M.) — Protective orders and sealing
docs.x: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough, D.N.M.. Protective orders and sealing: If all parties agree, file a stipulated motion with the proposed order attached and email a Word copy to the proposed-text address. If opposed, the opponent’s response must propose language resolving its specific objections. The order must give a basis for good cause under Rule 26(c), be narrowly tailored to named categories, and not limit the court’s discretion over confidential documents at hearings or trial. It may not contain a blanket sealing provision, bind non-parties automatically, provide continuing jurisdiction after the case ends, direct the Clerk to return or destroy filed documents, or bind court personnel or jurors. Designation as confidential does not overcome the presumption of public access; a party filing protected material in a pleading should also move to seal it.

docs.t: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough (D.N.M.) — Trial rules
docs.x: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough, D.N.M.. Trial rules: “Trial” means the initial jury selection date; extending any pretrial deadline requires leave, and a deadline on a weekend or holiday moves to the next working day. Multi-day trials recess about 5:00 p.m.; have witnesses to fill the 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. day. Stand when you speak, use surnames, stay within arm’s length of the podium, and make no speaking objections or argument of rulings before the jury. Give at least 2 weeks’ notice of audio-visual needs and schedule training with the Information Systems Help Desk (505-348-2110) at least 2 weeks before trial. Federal Bar Association WiFi is authorized during proceedings.

docs.t: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough (D.N.M.) — Witness and exhibit lists
docs.x: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough, D.N.M.. Witness and exhibit lists: Use the judge’s format: witnesses (or deposition designations) in the estimated order they will be called, with a brief description of testimony. Each party submits its own exhibit list showing number or letter, description, and whether stipulated, leaving the objection and admitted columns blank for the court.

docs.t: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough (D.N.M.) — Dress code
docs.x: Judge Steven C. Yarbrough, D.N.M.. Dress code: Witnesses, jurors, agents, and spectators: collared shirt and long pants, or a dress or blouse with a skirt or long pants (jeans acceptable); shoes required (no thongs); no shorts, t-shirts, or revealing clothing; hats off. Deviations need court approval before entering.

docs.t: Judge Michael D. Nelson (D. Neb.) — Detention reconsideration motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Michael D. Nelson, D. Neb.. Detention reconsideration motions (trap): A motion for reconsideration of detention must set out a release plan that follows the recommendations of a substance abuse evaluation and must state the positions of Probation and Pretrial Services and of the government. When the motion is filed, the defendant must also provide chambers with the substance abuse evaluation and a letter of acceptance from the proposed treatment program, with a statement of the program’s requirements.

docs.t: Judge Michael D. Nelson (D. Neb.) — Jury instructions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Michael D. Nelson, D. Neb.. Jury instructions (trap): Counsel must meet and confer, without the court, to build a complete joint set of instructions. At least two weeks before trial, file and email Word versions to chambers of a joint set of agreed instructions, a joint proposed verdict form, and, if needed, each party’s proposed instructions on disputed issues. Instructions must be jury-ready and tailored to the facts, not abstract propositions of law, and where possible based on the Eighth Circuit Model Civil Jury Instructions, the Nebraska Civil Jury Instructions, or other pattern instructions. The judge reads standard preliminary instructions after voir dire, holds an informal off-the-record instruction conference in chambers during trial followed by a formal one on the record, and gives final instructions after closing arguments.

docs.t: Judge Michael D. Nelson (D. Neb.) — Trial hours and time limits
docs.x: Judge Michael D. Nelson, D. Neb.. Trial hours and time limits: Trial usually runs 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. and 1:30 to 4:30 p.m., with 15-minute morning and afternoon breaks. Openings and closings are generally up to 30 minutes each; plaintiff may reserve up to 15 minutes of closing for true rebuttal only, with no new issues. The courtroom deputy keeps time and, on request, gives a 5-minute warning. In bench trials, openings and closings occur only if requested.

docs.t: Judge Michael D. Nelson (D. Neb.) — Jury selection and jurors
docs.x: Judge Michael D. Nelson, D. Neb.. Jury selection and jurors: The judge generally seats a 12-person civil jury unless counsel agree to fewer, with no alternates. After the judge’s limited examination, each party generally gets 20 minutes of voir dire. Jurors may take notes but may not ask or submit questions. Jury questions during deliberations are normally taken up on the record with counsel and parties present; stay reachable on short notice and keep the courtroom deputy informed of where you are until the verdict.

docs.t: Judge Michael D. Nelson (D. Neb.) — Examination and objections (trap)
docs.x: Judge Michael D. Nelson, D. Neb.. Examination and objections (trap): Re-cross examination is generally not allowed. Cross is limited to the scope of direct, and redirect to the scope of cross. No speaking objections in jury trials. For a foundation objection, state what foundation is lacking. Ask for a bench conference and allow time for the court reporter to set up; keep them to a minimum. Question from the podium unless directed otherwise, and refer to witnesses and parties by surname absent the judge’s permission. Plaintiff’s counsel use the tables nearest the jury box. Use the podium and table microphones about six inches away.

docs.t: Judge Michael D. Nelson (D. Neb.) — Exhibits and evidence presentation
docs.x: Judge Michael D. Nelson, D. Neb.. Exhibits and evidence presentation: When the exhibit list is delivered to the Clerk (NECivR 39.3), also give chambers a complete copy of the exhibits on a thumb drive or in a three-ring binder. Absent good cause, use the courtroom multimedia system, including the video presenter and your own laptops, to display exhibits, and get training from the courtroom deputy before trial. In jury trials the deputy generally controls publishing exhibits to the jury on the judge’s instruction.

docs.t: Judge Abizer Zanzi (N.D. Ind.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Abizer Zanzi, N.D. Ind.. Discovery disputes (trap): The court discourages formal motions to compel and motions for protective orders. After meeting and conferring under N.D. Ind. L.R. 37-1, file a Joint Motion for Discovery Ruling instead, no more than 5 pages. The joint motion should succinctly summarize each unresolved issue without extensive legal citation and state each party’s position and any proposed compromise. Attach the written discovery at issue (if any) and the parties’ prior correspondence on the issue. Only in the rare case where a joint motion is impossible may each party file its own Motion for Discovery Ruling, no more than 3 pages, filed simultaneously. The court will then promptly set a telephonic hearing, request further briefing, or tell the parties it will rule on the papers.

docs.t: Judge Abizer Zanzi (N.D. Ind.) — Recordings and transcripts
docs.x: Judge Abizer Zanzi, N.D. Ind.. Recordings and transcripts: Proceedings are recorded electronically on FTR Gold rather than by a court reporter. A copy of a recording costs $30.00, payable to the Clerk of Court; contact the case manager at 219-852-6707 to order one.

docs.t: Judge Abizer Zanzi (N.D. Ind.) — Jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Abizer Zanzi, N.D. Ind.. Jury instructions: The judge posts a set of general civil jury instructions covering the jury’s duties, evidence, direct and circumstantial evidence, credibility, impeachment, prior statements, preponderance of the evidence, deposition testimony, expert witnesses, and deliberations. The general instructions tell jurors that a corporate party is entitled to the same fair trial as an individual, that the verdict must be unanimous, that notes to the court must not reveal the jury’s numerical division, and that the court cannot supply trial transcripts.

docs.t: Judge Abizer Zanzi (N.D. Ind.) — Voir dire
docs.x: Judge Abizer Zanzi, N.D. Ind.. Voir dire: The judge’s general civil voir dire opens with a brief description of the case agreed to by the parties, has counsel introduce those at counsel table, and then asks individual background questions and panel-wide questions about the case, the parties, counsel, listed witnesses (read from the pretrial order), prior jury service, injuries, and claims. Counsel may submit additional questions; the court asks those and follow-up questions and then calls for challenges.

A defendant who will stipulate must notify chambers before the hearing date, orally through counsel or in writing, that the defendant agrees to probable cause, detention, or both and waives a hearing. If the defendant does not stipulate to detention, an in-person hearing will be set.

docs.t: Judge Scott J. Frankel (N.D. Ind.) — Preliminary pretrial conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott J. Frankel, N.D. Ind.. Preliminary pretrial conference (trap): Set about 30–60 days after the last party appears. Follow the Order of Preliminary Pretrial Conference and submit the Report of Parties’ Planning Meeting by the date it sets. Counsel must attend the Rule 16(b) conference in person. Only counsel from counties other than St. Joseph or Elkhart may appear by phone, and only on a motion that is granted. Be ready to describe the case, contentions, claims, and defenses, report on settlement, and discuss discovery. The court then issues a Scheduling Order and Memorandum of Status Conference, whose deadlines change only for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Scott J. Frankel (N.D. Ind.) — ESI protocol (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott J. Frankel, N.D. Ind.. ESI protocol (trap): The judge posts an ESI protocol template. Parties name e-discovery liaisons, exchange lists of ESI types and custodians to preserve, and agree on custodians, not more than 7 per party without leave. Sources not reasonably accessible (for example, backup media created before January 16, 2019, voicemail, and instant messaging) are preserved but not searched or produced absent leave on a showing of relevance and good cause. Metadata is excluded absent good cause, except date and time sent or received and the full distribution list. Produce in PDF (TIFF or JPEG by agreement for image-heavy documents), Bates-numbered, in unalterable form, without degrading searchability. Email requests should identify custodian, search terms, and time frame. The producing party bears the cost of assembling responses; a party that asks to examine a device

docs.t: Judge Scott J. Frankel (N.D. Ind.) — Pretrial filing deadlines (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott J. Frankel, N.D. Ind.. Pretrial filing deadlines (trap): Proposed jury instructions and voir dire questions: no later than 30 days before trial. Objections to them: at least 7 days before the final pretrial conference. Motions in limine: no later than 7 days before the final pretrial conference, filed in duplicate with memoranda. Bench trials: proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law at least 7 days before the final pretrial conference. Trial briefs are optional but, if filed, are due no later than 15 days before trial and must address each issue and element to be tried and anticipated evidentiary and legal questions, with citations.

docs.t: Judge Scott J. Frankel (N.D. Ind.) — Final pretrial conference
docs.x: Judge Scott J. Frankel, N.D. Ind.. Final pretrial conference: Normally held before all jury trials. Counsel must file a written pretrial order beforehand (see the Local Rules for contents), and all trial counsel must attend in person. Topics: pending motions, motions in limine, jury selection, exhibits, conduct of trial, and jury instructions. Unobjected-to exhibits may be admitted at the conference.

docs.t: Judge Scott J. Frankel (N.D. Ind.) — Exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott J. Frankel, N.D. Ind.. Exhibits (trap): No later than 20 days before trial, make copies of all potential exhibits, and all charts, graphs, models, or diagrams to be used at trial, available to opposing counsel. Bring three exhibit binders (court, witness, opposing counsel), plaintiff’s exhibits numbered and defendant’s lettered, with dividers. The witness binder holds the actual record exhibits and goes to the jury room; pull unadmitted exhibits at the close of evidence. Give the courtroom deputy an exhibit list at the start of trial. To publish an exhibit during trial, bring copies for each juror and the court if feasible. Material not disclosed this way cannot be used except to refresh recollection unless the need was unforeseeable and leave is obtained.

docs.t: Judge Scott J. Frankel (N.D. Ind.) — Witnesses and experts (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott J. Frankel, N.D. Ind.. Witnesses and experts (trap): The pretrial order must list the names, addresses, and occupations of all witnesses; no separate non-expert list is needed. Experts are disclosed under Rule 26(a)(2) and the scheduling order. Objections to an expert’s qualifications or foundation must be filed on or before the dispositive motions deadline, or they are waived. If counsel agree to waive qualification objections, the statement of qualifications need not be filed, but a statement of the substance of the testimony still must be.

docs.t: Judge Scott J. Frankel (N.D. Ind.) — Settlement and juror costs
docs.x: Judge Scott J. Frankel, N.D. Ind.. Settlement and juror costs: Parties must pursue settlement throughout the case. Under the district rule quoted on the page, if a jury case settles without notice to the clerk’s office at least one full business day before trial, juror costs may be assessed against the parties or counsel. Prior orders remain binding, and the issues may not be enlarged beyond the pretrial order or pleadings without an order expressly allowing it.

docs.x: Judge Scott J. Frankel, N.D. Ind.. docs.t: Judge Gilbert C. Sison (S.D. Ill.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gilbert C. Sison, S.D. Ill.. Discovery disputes (trap): Before the judge will consider any discovery matter, the party must certify a good-faith attempt to confer. If the dispute remains, the parties submit a one-page, non-argumentative joint statement of the issues with a brief outline of their efforts to resolve it, attaching any disputed written discovery and objections. Email the joint statement to GCSpd@ilsd.uscourts.gov and copy the courtroom deputy, Catina Simpson (Catina_Simpson@ilsd.uscourts.gov). The court then sets a discovery conference and may order expedited briefing with page limits (for example, a seven-day response and five-page briefs). Costs may be awarded against the non-prevailing party. Disputes referred by a district judge are handled as the district judge has directed.

docs.t: Judge Gilbert C. Sison (S.D. Ill.) — Motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gilbert C. Sison, S.D. Ill.. Motions (trap): Responses to dispositive motions, post-trial motions, and motions to remand are due in 30 days (L.R. 7.1(c)). Responsive memoranda are capped at 20 pages without written leave. Replies are strongly discouraged; if filed, 5 pages, within 14 days of service of the response. A motion to dismiss must state the exact subsection (for example, Rule 12(b)(6), not “Rule 12(b)”), whether it targets the complaint, the whole case, or particular parties or claims, and whether dismissal is sought with or without prejudice. Hearings are set at the judge’s discretion; counsel may move for one. After e-filing an urgent or time-sensitive motion, tell the courtroom deputy or the assigned law clerk. All Daubert motions are due by the dispositive motion deadline, not the motion in limine deadline; late ones will be denied as untimely.

docs.t: Judge Gilbert C. Sison (S.D. Ill.) — Disclosures and conflicts
docs.x: Judge Gilbert C. Sison, S.D. Ill.. Disclosures and conflicts: Rule 26(a)(3) pretrial disclosures are due 4 weeks before the scheduled final pretrial conference (not 30 days before trial), with objections 2 weeks later, all e-filed. Objections are taken up at the final pretrial conference. Non-governmental parties must make Rule 7.1 disclosures and update them, and except in class actions must list all parties in the caption so the judge can check for conflicts.

docs.t: Judge Gilbert C. Sison (S.D. Ill.) — Rule 16 and telephonic appearances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gilbert C. Sison, S.D. Ill.. Rule 16 and telephonic appearances (trap): Submit the joint report at least 7 days before the scheduling conference as one report, on the form for cases referred to mandatory mediation, not referred, or class actions. The conference is telephonic and usually still held; its purposes are to plan for difficult discovery issues and to schedule a settlement conference, identifying the least discovery needed for settlement. Treat telephonic hearings as in-person and be punctual. Missing one draws a show-cause order; missing another revokes the privilege, and all later appearances must be in person.

docs.t: Judge Gilbert C. Sison (S.D. Ill.) — Settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Gilbert C. Sison, S.D. Ill.. Settlement conferences: Usually set at the Rule 16 conference, starting at 9:00 a.m. and possibly lasting all day. Lead counsel and the parties must attend; an insured individual defendant may instead send an insurer representative with full authority, meaning someone who can agree to any sum demanded without calling anyone. Relief from attendance is unlikely. In employment cases, leave behind anyone who had input in the challenged decision when possible. Defendants who bring only nuisance money may have to pay plaintiff’s costs of attending. Email settlement statements to GCSpd@ilsd.uscourts.gov (not CM/ECF) 7 days before the conference. If negotiations look futile, contact chambers immediately.

docs.t: Judge Gilbert C. Sison (S.D. Ill.) — Final pretrial order and exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gilbert C. Sison, S.D. Ill.. Final pretrial order and exhibits (trap): Use the judge’s Final Pretrial Order form (mandatory) and email the signed joint order to GCSpd@ilsd.uscourts.gov no later than 3 days before the final pretrial conference. The court reads the statement of the case to the venire. Witnesses not listed in the order generally may not testify. Motions in limine are due 21 days before the final pretrial conference, with responses within 7 days. Late motions may be stricken if they would delay trial. Trial briefs are optional; if filed, they are due 14 days before trial and may not rehash issues already decided. Submit the exhibit list on the approved form (a revision of AO 187) at least 4 business days before trial. Use numbers only, with no letter suffixes, no group exhibits, and a separate number for each photograph; multi-page exhibits get one number with page ref

docs.t: Judge Gilbert C. Sison (S.D. Ill.) — Jury instructions (trap)

docs.t: Judge Martin C. Carlson (M.D. Pa.) — Contact

docs.t: Judge Phillip Caraballo (M.D. Pa.) — Discovery disputes (trap)

docs.t: Judge Phillip Caraballo (M.D. Pa.) — Letters and motions (trap)

docs.t: Judge Phillip Caraballo (M.D. Pa.) — Conferences, contact, and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Phillip Caraballo, M.D. Pa.. docs.t: Judge Phillip Caraballo (M.D. Pa.) — Generative AI
docs.x: Judge Phillip Caraballo, M.D. Pa.. docs.t: Judge Phillip Caraballo (M.D. Pa.) — Case schedules and extensions
docs.x: Judge Phillip Caraballo, M.D. Pa.. docs.t: Judge Phillip Caraballo (M.D. Pa.) — Confidentiality and admissions

docs.t: Judge Phillip Caraballo (M.D. Pa.) — Pretrial and trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Phillip Caraballo, M.D. Pa.. Pretrial and trial (trap): A date certain for trial is set at the final pretrial conference. docs.t: Judge Phillip Caraballo (M.D. Pa.) — Settlement

docs.t: Judge Sean A. Camoni (M.D. Pa.) — Discovery disputes by letter (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sean A. Camoni, M.D. Pa.. docs.t: Judge Sean A. Camoni (M.D. Pa.) — Generative AI certificate (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sean A. Camoni, M.D. Pa.. Parties and counsel must also review the conclusions on pages 15 and 16 of the Joint Formal Opinion of the Pennsylvania Bar Association and Philadelphia Bar Association on AI.

docs.t: Judge Sean A. Camoni (M.D. Pa.) — Correspondence and contact (trap)

docs.t: Judge Sean A. Camoni (M.D. Pa.) — Conferences and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Sean A. Camoni, M.D. Pa.. docs.t: Judge Sean A. Camoni (M.D. Pa.) — Case schedules and extensions
docs.x: Judge Sean A. Camoni, M.D. Pa.. docs.t: Judge Sean A. Camoni (M.D. Pa.) — Trial scheduling

docs.t: Judge Sean A. Camoni (M.D. Pa.) — Pretrial and trial
docs.x: Judge Sean A. Camoni, M.D. Pa.. Pretrial and trial: Trial briefs are due, as the local rules require, before the final pretrial conference. docs.t: Judge Susan E. Schwab (M.D. Pa.) — Correspondence and discovery disputes (trap)

docs.t: Judge Susan E. Schwab (M.D. Pa.) — Contact and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Susan E. Schwab, M.D. Pa.. docs.t: Judge Susan E. Schwab (M.D. Pa.) — Case schedules and extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Susan E. Schwab, M.D. Pa.. docs.t: Judge Susan E. Schwab (M.D. Pa.) — Discovery and confidentiality

docs.t: Judge Susan E. Schwab (M.D. Pa.) — Trial scheduling
docs.x: Judge Susan E. Schwab, M.D. Pa.. Trial scheduling: Whenever possible, a date certain for jury selection is set in the initial case management order, typically the third Monday of the month. Non-jury trials are set for a date certain after consulting counsel.

docs.t: Judge Susan E. Schwab (M.D. Pa.) — Pretrial and trial
docs.x: Judge Susan E. Schwab, M.D. Pa.. Pretrial and trial: Trial briefs are due, as the local rules require, before the final pretrial conference. Civil voir dire is conducted by the court, usually with counsel’s pre-approved supplemental questions; in criminal cases the court conducts all of voir dire. More than one attorney may try a case for a party. Submit proposed jury instructions under the local rules; a jointly prepared, agreed special verdict slip is strongly encouraged.

docs.t: Judge Susan E. Schwab (M.D. Pa.) — Settlement and consent
docs.x: Judge Susan E. Schwab, M.D. Pa.. Settlement and consent: Settlement is pursued thoroughly in jury cases; settlement discussions in non-jury cases are referred to another judge. Consent to a magistrate judge is encouraged.

docs.t: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung (D. Colo.) — Chambers contact and courtroom
docs.x: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung, D. Colo.. Chambers contact and courtroom: Procedural questions go by email to Chung_Chambers@cod.uscourts.gov, copying opposing counsel or pro se parties. Chambers will not discuss substantive matters or grant informal requests not made by motion. For trial, contact the courtroom deputy at least 14 days ahead about remote witnesses (if allowed), exhibits, witness lists, courtroom procedures, and a technical walk-through. Requests for realtime or daily rough transcripts must be made at least 30 days before trial. The public obtains dial-in information for telephonic hearings from the courtroom deputy.

docs.t: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung (D. Colo.) — Final pretrial order and trial length
docs.x: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung, D. Colo.. Final pretrial order and trial length: Counsel must meet at least 14 days before the Final Pretrial Conference; plaintiff’s counsel (defense counsel if plaintiff is pro se) schedules the meetings and files the order, unless delegated by agreement. File the proposed Final Pretrial Order 7 days before the conference and email a Word version to chambers. A request for a trial longer than five days must be justified by argument before a trial date is set.

docs.t: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung (D. Colo.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung, D. Colo.. Motions in limine (trap): Discouraged when the issue cannot be resolved until evidence is presented; flag such issues in a trial brief instead. Confer first and decide which party files on each issue. Each party gets one motion in limine, with each dispute separately numbered; motion and response are capped at 8 pages (all text counts except signature blocks and certificate of service), and no replies. Motions are due 21 days and responses 14 days before the Trial Preparation Conference.

docs.t: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung (D. Colo.) — Trial Preparation Conference
docs.x: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung, D. Colo.. Trial Preparation Conference: Usually about 14 days before trial; counsel who will try the case must attend. File proposed voir dire 7 days before, omitting routine questions the court already asks. Raise any request for a jury questionnaire, or for more time for voir dire, openings, or closings, at the conference.

docs.t: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung (D. Colo.) — Jury instructions and verdict form (trap)
docs.x: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung, D. Colo.. Jury instructions and verdict form (trap): Due 21 days before the Trial Preparation Conference, by email to chambers in Word, NOT filed on CM/ECF. Plaintiff’s counsel (defense counsel if plaintiff is pro se) sends the stipulated set and verdict form; each proffering party sends its own competing and non-stipulated instructions. Label each instruction at the bottom as Stipulated, Competing, or Non-Stipulated (and by party), and for disputed ones add one paragraph of argument from each side with authority; no separate objections. Do not number instructions; center a bold title, redline or describe edits to pattern instructions, and use hard page breaks. The court generally follows Federal Jury Practice and Instructions and the Colorado Jury Instructions – Civil, and posts template instructions it gives in every trial. Capitalize “Court,” and refer to parties

docs.t: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung (D. Colo.) — Exhibits and witness lists (trap)
docs.x: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung, D. Colo.. Exhibits and witness lists (trap): Use the judge’s posted forms. Plaintiffs number exhibits and defendants use letters; put the case number on every sticker and number pages of unpaginated exhibits over two pages. Exhibit and witness lists are filed 7 days before the Trial Preparation Conference, and final lists by noon the Friday before trial. Two days after witness lists are filed, file estimates of cross-examination time; final witness lists give direct and cross estimates. Oversized exhibits need prior approval. By 9:00 a.m. at least two business days before trial, each side delivers one USB flash drive and three exhibit notebooks (labeled original or copy) to the courtroom deputy, after emailing chambers for delivery instructions. Improperly bound or labeled exhibits can delay or continue the trial.

docs.t: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung (D. Colo.) — Depositions and glossary
docs.x: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung, D. Colo.. Depositions and glossary: Exchange designations 30 days before trial (plaintiff yellow, defendant blue, others green); counter-designations and objections 21 days before; submit the highlighted transcript to chambers, with objections in red and the basis and response noted, 14 days before trial. Video proponents must be able to mute excluded answers and skip ahead. In bench trials, the court reads designated depositions in chambers; provide two marked copies at the start of trial. Email chambers a glossary of technical terms, names, and acronyms 5 business days before trial, and bring three paper copies on the first day.

docs.t: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung (D. Colo.) — Jury trials
docs.x: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung, D. Colo.. Jury trials: Day one starts at 8:00 a.m., with jury selection at 8:30 a.m.; later days run 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Juries are normally nine (eight plus one alternate), with three peremptories per side. After the court’s initial voir dire, counsel get 30 minutes per party or party group. Openings are 30 minutes and closings 60 minutes per party or party group; exchange demonstratives for opening 3 business days before trial. Jurors may take notes and submit written questions for witnesses, which the court may read, modify, or reject after a bench conference. One attorney per witness and for voir dire and opening; two may split closing only when a party has two closings.

docs.t: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung (D. Colo.) — Bench trials and trial briefs
docs.x: Judge Cyrus Y. Chung, D. Colo.. Bench trials and trial briefs: File proposed findings of fact, conclusions of law, and orders at least 2 business days before the Trial Preparation Conference and email them in Word, ordered to track the expected order of proof. A marked résumé or CV generally suffices to qualify an expert. Trial briefs are optional, capped at 10 pages, due 5 days before the Trial Preparation Conference, and cannot substitute for a motion.

docs.t: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell (D. Colo.) — Chambers and courtroom
docs.x: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell, D. Colo.. Chambers and courtroom: Questions about these procedures go by email to Braswell_chambers@cod.uscourts.gov, copying all counsel and pro se parties; courtroom technology questions go to the courtroom deputy. The Colorado Springs courtroom is small. Proceedings are recorded; no court reporter is assigned unless the parties expressly ask, and coverage is not guaranteed for trials over four days. A privately hired reporter’s transcript is not the official record.

docs.t: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell (D. Colo.) — Motions in limine and bifurcation (trap)
docs.x: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell, D. Colo.. Motions in limine and bifurcation (trap): Unless the court sets other terms, motions in limine are due 10 days before the Final Pretrial Conference and responses 3 days before; motions are capped at 5 pages, responses at 3, and no replies. Confer first. Motions to bifurcate are due 21 days before the Final Pretrial Order is due.

docs.t: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell (D. Colo.) — Final Pretrial Conference
docs.x: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell, D. Colo.. Final Pretrial Conference: File the proposed Final Pretrial Order at least 7 days before, after meaningful conferral, and email a Word version to chambers. Come ready to give an overview of pending issues with proposed solutions, confirm conferral on exhibit authenticity and admissibility, justify any trial over five days, address non-electronic exhibits (electronic is preferred), Rule 1006 charts, deposition designations, jury questionnaires, pre- or post-trial briefs, technology, and settlement prospects, and argue motions in limine.

docs.t: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell (D. Colo.) — Submissions due 4 days before the Trial Preparation Conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell, D. Colo.. Submissions due 4 days before the Trial Preparation Conference (trap): Filed on CM/ECF: the joint exhibit list (Appendix A form; authenticity objections expected only rarely) and the joint witness list with direct and cross estimates (Appendix B form). Emailed to chambers in Word: two joint case statements (a short one for prospective jurors and one with uncontested facts for the preliminary instructions, with no evidence offered in either), joint proposed jury instructions, a joint verdict form (or competing forms if no agreement), and each side’s proposed voir dire questions. Deposition designations are discussed at the Final Pretrial Conference; then email a joint Deposition Designation Chart (Appendix C form) and a hard-copy transcript (proponent yellow, counter-designations green).

docs.t: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell (D. Colo.) — Jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell, D. Colo.. Jury instructions: Model instructions and special-interrogatory verdict forms are encouraged, written for laypersons. Where the parties disagree, plaintiff offers its instruction and the objecting party states its basis and a competing instruction immediately below, in underlined font. The court gives preliminary views at the Trial Preparation Conference and rules after a charging conference. Final instructions are read before closing, and each juror gets a copy.

docs.t: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell (D. Colo.) — Jury selection (trap)
docs.x: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell, D. Colo.. Jury selection (trap): Eight jurors including one alternate. After the court’s initial voir dire, each side gets 15 minutes, limited to pre-approved questions and follow-ups; underline any proposed questions you want the court to ask instead. Avoid irrelevant personal questions (such as political affiliation), questions about anyone beyond immediate family or household, and questions that prejudge evidence, seek commitments on hypotheticals, or plant inadmissible matters. Cause challenges are made at sidebar, never in front of the panel. Each side has 3 peremptory strikes on a court-prepared strike list; Batson challenges must be made after all strikes and before the jury is sworn.

docs.t: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell (D. Colo.) — Trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell, D. Colo.. Trial (trap): Day one begins at 8:00 a.m.; on other days counsel arrive by 8:30 a.m. and the jury is called at 9:00 a.m., with dismissal around 4:30 p.m. and the last half hour for housekeeping. Rule 615 motions are made then. Openings are limited to 25 minutes and closings to 35, absent leave. Pretrial rulings are not self-executing: object at trial to enforce an exclusion until the court says further objections are unnecessary. Bring one USB flash drive of pre-marked exhibits (marked as plaintiff’s or defendant’s) to the courtroom deputy on day one, and confer with the deputy daily on admitted exhibits. Jurors get notes, a copy of the instructions, and a computer loaded with admitted exhibits for deliberations. Motions under Local Civil Rule 47.2 to talk with jurors after the verdict must be made before the last day of trial, outside the jury

docs.t: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell (D. Colo.) — Bench trials
docs.x: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell, D. Colo.. Bench trials: At least 7 days before the Final Pretrial Conference, file (and email in Word) joint proposed findings of fact, with challenges set out underlined below each disputed fact, and each side’s own proposed conclusions of law, citing the joint findings. Within 10 days after trial, file revised versions with a proposed order or judgment. A marked résumé or CV generally suffices to qualify an expert.

docs.t: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell (D. Colo.) — Artificial intelligence
docs.x: Judge Maritza Dominguez Braswell, D. Colo.. Artificial intelligence: Judge Dominguez Braswell has deliberately issued no AI standing order: there is no ban and no certification requirement. The posted guidance is expressly not an order and creates no new rules. It recommends verifying all AI output outside the tool, conferring early on protective-order terms and on AI in discovery and ESI protocols, and disclosing AI use that could affect evaluation (for example, AI-generated demonstratives). For an opponent’s apparent hallucination, it suggests conferring, jointly informing the court, and filing a notice only if the drafter will not engage; prompt self-correction of your own errors is encouraged.

docs.t: Judge N. Reid Neureiter (D. Colo.) — AI certification on every filing (trap)
docs.x: Judge N. Reid Neureiter, D. Colo.. AI certification on every filing (trap): In consent cases, every filing must contain an AI Certification on the use or non-use of generative AI, signed by everyone who helped draft it. If AI was used, each signer certifies that all AI-drafted language (even if later edited) was reviewed by a human for accuracy and that every citation is to real authority. The certification does not count against page limits. In referral cases, it applies only to referred opposed motions.

docs.t: Judge N. Reid Neureiter (D. Colo.) — AI sanctions
docs.x: Judge N. Reid Neureiter, D. Colo.. AI sanctions: The court will strike any filing that lacks a compliant certification, and in appropriate cases will consider awarding attorney fees to the opposing party when an AI-assisted filing lacked substantial justification. Rule 11, 28 U.S.C. § 1927, and ethics rules still apply. Counsel are encouraged to review Judge Dominguez Braswell’s AI guidance.

docs.t: Judge N. Reid Neureiter (D. Colo.) — Rule 30(b)(6) notices
docs.x: Judge N. Reid Neureiter, D. Colo.. Rule 30(b)(6) notices: The guidance stresses cooperation: the noticing party must describe topics with painstaking, case-specific particularity, and the organization must produce fully prepared witnesses on each proper topic. Overbroad notices, “including but not limited to” language, and memory-test questioning are disfavored. Since 2020, the parties must confer about the matters for examination before or promptly after service, and a subpoena to a nonparty organization must notify it of the duty to confer and designate.

docs.t: Judge N. Reid Neureiter (D. Colo.) — Rule 30(b)(6) scope and time
docs.x: Judge N. Reid Neureiter, D. Colo.. Rule 30(b)(6) scope and time: Questions beyond the noticed topics are allowed, but answers bind only the individual; note scope objections on the record rather than instructing the witness not to answer. Do not assume a fresh seven hours per designee; most judges allow little or no extra time, so seek agreement or a ruling. Prior individual depositions do not bar a 30(b)(6) deposition (or vice versa), and either may come first. Legal contentions are not entirely off-limits, though contention interrogatories are usually better.

docs.t: Judge N. Reid Neureiter (D. Colo.) — Problem topics to avoid
docs.x: Judge N. Reid Neureiter, D. Colo.. Problem topics to avoid: The guidance gives examples of improper topics, such as “all facts and documents” supporting defenses or counterclaims, the identity of all persons with knowledge of every other topic, and sprawling multi-part topics about claim-note practices.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — AI certification (trap)
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. AI certification (trap): In consent cases, every Rule 12 motion, Rule 56 motion, motion to amend, and opposed motion (and its response and reply) must include, besides the conferral certificate, a certification that no part was drafted by generative AI or that all AI-drafted language was reviewed by a human for accuracy using print reporters or traditional legal databases, with citations confirmed real. The court will strike a covered filing that lacks the certification. In referral cases, the rule applies only to referred nondispositive, opposed motions.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — Rule 502(d) order
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. Rule 502(d) order: The judge posts a form stipulated order providing that producing privileged or work-product material, inadvertently or otherwise, waives nothing in this or any other proceeding, with maximum protection under Fed. R. Evid. 502(d), while preserving each party’s right to review before production.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — Final Pretrial/Trial Preparation Conference
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. Final Pretrial/Trial Preparation Conference: Usually one combined conference about six weeks before trial; trial counsel must attend in person, and an incarcerated pro se party normally appears by phone. Be ready to discuss trial length and show good cause for more than five days. File the proposed Final Pretrial Order (district form) 7 days before and email a Word version to Prose_Chambers@cod.uscourts.gov; in pro se cases represented parties take the lead. Each side’s proposed voir dire is filed and emailed in Word 7 days before.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — Motions in limine and trial briefs (trap)
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. Motions in limine and trial briefs (trap): One omnibus motion in limine per party, capped at 20 pages, due 42 days before the conference; responses are due 28 days before or 14 days after filing, whichever is earlier. No replies without leave and good cause. Trial briefs are optional, capped at 10 pages, due 5 days before the conference, and cannot substitute for a motion.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — Jury instructions and verdict form
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. Jury instructions and verdict form: Due 14 days before the conference, filed jointly (instructions and verdict form separately) and emailed in Word. One instruction per page, numbered, with source and authority. For each disputed instruction, each party submits its own, plus a single joint redline showing the competing language. Stipulate to a verdict form understandable to laypersons. Capitalize party names without articles (“Plaintiff”) and use titles (Ms., Mr., Dr.) rather than bare last names.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — Exhibits and witnesses (trap)
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. Exhibits and witnesses (trap): Use the judge’s joint exhibit and witness list formats, filed and emailed in Word 7 days before the conference; stipulate to authenticity and admissibility as much as possible, or risk further conferences or a reset trial date. Also 7 days before, jointly deliver an exhibit notebook to the courtroom deputy, with numbered tabs, color where the original is in color, internal page numbers, and sequential numbering with no plaintiff or defendant attribution. Bring two USB drives of pre-marked exhibits on day one. Estimate time for every examination; the totals must fit within each side’s allotted time, and the estimates are strictly enforced. On day one bring three paper copies of a final witness list with time estimates.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — Depositions and glossary
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. Depositions and glossary: Designations are due 21 days before the conference and counter-designations 14 days before, exchanged but not filed. After conferring, file and email a joint objection chart (page and line, explanation, case law) and email the transcripts, with each party’s designations in a different color and a legend, 7 days before. Video proponents must be able to mute excluded answers and skip ahead, or the testimony will be read. Email chambers a joint glossary of technical terms and names 5 business days before trial and bring three paper copies on day one.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — Demonstratives (trap)
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. Demonstratives (trap): Demonstratives must be prepared outside court; none may be created during trial, none may contain unadmitted documents even if stipulated, and none go to the jury room. Exchange slides for opening 2 business days before trial and for closing by 6:00 p.m. the evening before, sending copies to chambers. Do not use unstipulated documents in opening or unadmitted documents in closing.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — Jury trials
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. Jury trials: Be present by 8:30 a.m. daily; trial runs about 9:00 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. Civil juries have at least 7 jurors, who may take notes and get a copy of the instructions, which are read before closing. After the court’s voir dire, each side gets 30 minutes; three peremptory strikes per side. Openings are generally 30 minutes per party, closings as the court sets; typically one attorney per party for each, and plaintiff must ask to reserve rebuttal time before closing.

docs.t: Judge Susan Prose (D. Colo.) — Bench trials
docs.x: Judge Susan Prose, D. Colo.. Bench trials: Openings are generally limited to 20 minutes and closings to 30; by agreement a written submission of up to 10 pages may replace closing. File joint proposed findings, conclusions, and orders for stipulated points, plus each party’s own for disputed points, 3 business days before the conference, citing trial exhibits and law, in order of proof, and email Word versions. A marked résumé or CV generally suffices for expert qualification.

docs.t: Judge Caroline H. Gentry (S.D. Ohio) — Civil scheduling in consent cases (trap)
docs.x: Judge Caroline H. Gentry, S.D. Ohio. Civil scheduling in consent cases (trap): The judge’s form Rule 16(b) order keys deadlines to the filing of the Rule 26(f) report: initial disclosures 2 weeks after; plaintiff’s settlement demand 1 month after; defendant’s response 2 months after; motions directed to the pleadings (for example, to amend or add parties) and lay witness lists with synopses 3 months after. Experts run backward from the discovery cutoff: plaintiff’s primary experts 4 months before, defendant’s 3 months before; plaintiff’s rebuttal experts 2 months before, defendant’s 1 month before. Counsel and unrepresented parties must also follow S.D. Ohio (Dayton) General Order 12-1.

docs.t: Judge Caroline H. Gentry (S.D. Ohio) — Civil dispositive motions and trial deadlines
docs.x: Judge Caroline H. Gentry, S.D. Ohio. Civil dispositive motions and trial deadlines: Discovery closes 6 months before trial and summary judgment motions are due 5 months before trial. Written motions in limine are due 3 weeks before trial; the Joint Final Pretrial Order 1 week before the final pretrial conference; trial exhibits are exchanged 3 days before it; and jury instructions and verdict forms are due 1 week before trial. The final pretrial conference is held in chambers 1 week before trial, and sets of exhibits go to chambers 3 business days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Caroline H. Gentry (S.D. Ohio) — Newer attorneys (civil)
docs.x: Judge Caroline H. Gentry, S.D. Ohio. Newer attorneys (civil): Newer attorneys (in practice six years or less) are strongly encouraged to argue motions and examine witnesses, and the judge will allow multiple lawyers to argue or present evidence for one client to make that possible. After a civil motion is fully briefed or an informal discovery dispute is raised, any party may file a docketed Notice that a newer attorney will argue it if oral argument is granted. A similar Notice may be filed before an evidentiary hearing or trial; more experienced counsel of record may assist.

docs.t: Judge Caroline H. Gentry (S.D. Ohio) — Petty-offense criminal cases: discovery and motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Caroline H. Gentry, S.D. Ohio. Petty-offense criminal cases: discovery and motions (trap): Bench trials are set on a Monday at 9:00 a.m. (and the following Tuesday if needed). Defense counsel must arrange a discovery meeting with the AUSA no later than 14 days after arraignment. Motions to compel discovery must be filed within one week of a party’s denial of a request. A motion to continue trial must be written, filed about ten days before trial, state whether it is opposed, and show good cause. All other written motions are due about three weeks before trial, oppositions one week after filing, and no replies without leave; each motion must say whether an evidentiary hearing is requested. Oral motions in limine may be made any time before the close of evidence.

docs.x: Judge Caroline H. Gentry, S.D. Ohio. docs.x: Judge Karen L. Litkovitz, S.D. Ohio. docs.x: Judge Karen L. Litkovitz, S.D. Ohio. Refer to prospective jurors by seat number; counsel may supplement but not repeat the court’s voir dire. Examine from the lectern, ask permission to approach a witness, one attorney per witness, stand to object and state grounds only if asked, and no colloquy between counsel. Jury instructions and exhibits: Use Ninth Circuit models, then CACI or BAJI for California law; each instruction on a separate numbered page with its source, and an index. File agreed instructions, then each side’s disputed instructions with short supporting and opposing statements; email Word versions. The court gives its own introductory instructions. Exhibits tagged lower right and internally paginated; for paper exhibits, two binder sets for the court and one for opponent. An exhibit conference with trial counsel is held at 1:30 p.m. the Friday before trial, unless ordered otherwise.

docs.t: Judge A. Joel Richlin (C.D. Cal.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge A. Joel Richlin, C.D. Cal.. Trial: Jury trial days generally Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., with three 15-minute breaks and no lunch break; on the first day, counsel go on the record at 8:30 a.m. and selection starts at 9:00 a.m. Later, matters outside the jury’s presence are handled 8:15 to 8:30 a.m. Sidebars are discouraged. Usually eight jurors and three peremptories per side, by the Arizona blind-strike method; each side gets up to 20 minutes of follow-up voir dire. Use the lectern; state objections and legal grounds only. Lodge depositions with the courtroom deputy on the first day of trial. A party without a next witness may be deemed to have rested.
